metadata.narrative: I’m the technical founder of a 35-person B2B software startup. We have product-market fit, a seed extension, and growing enterprise demand, but I’m getting pulled into fundraising, hiring, finance, sales escalations, and internal process issues instead of product. A board member suggested either hiring a COO now or planning for a professional CEO later, and I’m worried about losing control or damaging the culture. How should I think about staying CEO versus bringing in experienced management, and what should I put in place over the next 12 months?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Given your stage, this is not a binary choice between staying CEO and bringing in a professional CEO; it is a sequence of role changes most founder-CEOs go through, and the right first move is almost certainly a COO, not a CEO swap.

Operators who have made this hire flag that a COO becomes necessary once operational complexity outgrows the existing team, and this typically lines up with a Series A raise or a headcount around thirty, which matches your situation closely.

The right COO profile has strong strategy-and-operations experience and can act autonomously on execution while still treating big strategic calls as a joint decision with you, rather than being a micromanager who tries to run everything personally.

A useful way to think about your own job changing is the three-phase model of founder-CEO evolution: Phase One is building product and finding early users, while Phase Two, starting around twenty to twenty-five employees and running until a company reaches the hundreds, requires you to shift into hiring a leadership team, creating alignment, and nurturing culture rather than doing the work yourself.

A complementary framework for SaaS companies moving from roughly thirty to a hundred employees describes the same shift concretely: the CEO stops having day-to-day execution responsibility and instead holds onto only three things that cannot be delegated, setting company strategy, hiring the top leaders who then hire everyone else, and making sure there is enough cash to run the business.

That framing should reassure you that fundraising, hiring senior leaders, and cash management remain legitimately your job even after you delegate a COO the sales escalations, finance operations, and internal process work currently pulling you away from product.

Before making any structural change, audit your calendar, because where a CEO spends time is described as an investment decision, and the recommended fix includes creating a real timesheet, reallocating blocks to the highest-leverage activities, admitting which tasks you lack the skill set for, and considering intermediate options such as a CEO peer group, an advisory board, or a contract COO before jumping straight to an outside CEO.

Your instinct to worry about losing control is not irrational: research cited by longtime operators shows that a large share of founding CEOs are replaced after later funding rounds, with the substantial majority of removals initiated by the board rather than chosen by the founder.

High-profile examples of founders pushed out of the CEO seat illustrate how board composition shifts after venture funding can dilute founder control if it isn't actively managed, since roughly half of founding CEOs are reportedly terminated within eighteen months of a Series A.

The same research offers a hopeful counterpoint: CEOs who proactively put in place their own succession plan are far more likely to remain on the board and retain a real executive role afterward, and their equity stakes tend to increase in value when they hire a strong successor.

Reid Hoffman's argument for why founders eventually bring in outside leadership is that CEOs need to derive satisfaction from the nuts and bolts of building a company, not just product and vision, as the company scales, which is exactly the tension you are describing.

Because of that dynamic, hiring a COO under your authority, on your timeline, with a scope you define, is the lower-risk path relative to waiting and letting the board force a CEO change later, and bringing in senior leadership at this stage is explicitly framed as not being a demotion for the founder.

On governance, a well-run seed-to-Series-A board has five core functions, helping hire and mentor the CEO, shaping strategy, approving the operating budget, monitoring performance, and fulfilling fiduciary oversight, and should explicitly avoid meddling in day-to-day operations.

Use your next board conversation to get written agreement on decision rights and committee structure, since a typical board of five to seven members with standing finance/audit, compensation, and governance committees is the norm at this stage.

On culture, the risk is real but manageable: as companies add distributed employees, culture stops being something people absorb by osmosis and must be deliberately articulated, and a practical approach is to identify the four to six values the founder genuinely believes, that attract talent, and that help customers, write them down, build and repeat stories that illustrate them, model them visibly, and use them explicitly in hiring, promotion, and firing decisions.

Founders who have handed off responsibility describe the emotional difficulty honestly, and the advice is to maintain a healthy distance from delegated areas rather than reflexively reinserting yourself, finding confidence in knowing the incoming leaders share your vision and values; one profiled founder even transitioned fully from CEO to president emeritus, showing that stepping back does not mean losing influence over direction or culture.

Common founder-transition mistakes around this size include being afraid to hire senior people early, falling into hero mode and refusing to delegate, delegating badly by withholding real decision-making authority, and lacking personal organization systems to track your own commitments.
For the next twelve months, follow this sequence.
First, run the time audit and formally decide which non-delegable jobs you keep: strategy, top hires, and cash.

Second, hire a COO scoped explicitly around finance operations, hiring processes, sales escalations, and internal process issues, screening for autonomy and operational strength rather than a need to control every detail.
Third, put your own succession thinking in front of the board proactively, including clear written decision rights and committee structure, so you are driving governance rather than reacting to it.

Fourth, document your leadership-hiring plan, org structure, and reporting lines now, before crossing into headcounts where undocumented structure becomes far harder to fix, while avoiding hero mode and bad delegation as you do it.
Fifth, write down your core values with real stories and start using them explicitly in hiring and performance decisions before the culture fragments across new hires.

Sixth, revisit this plan with the board every few months, treating a founder-CEO who built a proactive succession plan as the identity you are actively choosing, since that posture is associated with founders retaining both influence and equity value rather than being pushed out involuntarily.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

output.text:
Given your stage, this is not a binary choice between “stay CEO” and “bring in a professional CEO”; it is a sequence of role changes that most founder-CEOs go through, and the right first move is almost certainly a COO, not a CEO swap.

Operators who have made this hire specifically flag that a COO becomes necessary once operational complexity outgrows the existing team, and they note this typically lines up with a Series A raise or a headcount around thirty, which matches your situation almost exactly.

The right COO profile is someone with strong strategy-and-operations experience who can act autonomously on execution while still treating big strategic calls as a joint decision with you, rather than a micromanager who tries to run everything personally.

A useful way to think about your own job changing is the three-phase model of founder-CEO evolution: Phase One is “Doer-in-Chief,” building product and finding early users; Phase Two, which typically starts around twenty to twenty-five employees and runs until a company reaches the hundreds, requires you to become “Company-Builder-in-Chief,” meaning your job becomes hiring a leadership team, creating alignment, and nurturing culture rather than doing the work yourself.

A complementary framework for SaaS companies moving from roughly thirty to a hundred employees describes the same shift concretely: the CEO stops having day-to-day responsibility for execution and instead holds onto only three things that cannot be delegated—setting company strategy, hiring the top leaders who then hire everyone else, and making sure there is enough cash to run the business, which in a fundraising environment can consume the majority of a CEO’s time.

That framing should reassure you that fundraising, hiring senior leaders, and cash management are legitimately still your job even after you delegate a COO the sales escalations, finance operations, and internal process work that are currently pulling you away from product.

Before making any structural change, it is worth literally auditing your calendar, because where a CEO spends time is described as an investment decision, and the recommended fix set includes creating a real timesheet, reallocating blocks to the highest-leverage activities, admitting which tasks you lack the skill set for and handing those off, and considering intermediate options such as a CEO peer group, an advisory board, or a contract COO before jumping straight to bringing in a full outside CEO.

Your instinct to worry about losing control is not irrational: research cited by longtime operators shows that a large share of founding CEOs are replaced after later funding rounds, with the substantial majority of those removals initiated by the board rather than chosen by the founder, and high-profile examples of founders pushed out of the CEO seat illustrate how board composition shifts after venture funding can dilute founder control if it isn’t actively managed.

The same research base offers a more hopeful counterpoint, though: CEOs who proactively put in place their own succession plan are far more likely to remain on the board and retain a real executive role afterward, and their equity stakes tend to increase in value when they hire a strong successor, which argues for you driving this transition deliberately now rather than waiting for the board to force it later.

Because of that dynamic, hiring a COO under your authority, on your timeline, with a scope you define, is the lower-risk path relative to “planning for a professional CEO later,” since the latter framing implicitly cedes the initiative to the board.

On governance, a well-run seed-to-Series-A board has five core functions—helping hire and mentor the CEO, shaping strategy, approving the operating budget, monitoring performance, and fulfilling fiduciary oversight—and should explicitly avoid meddling in day-to-day operations, so it is worth using your next board conversation to get written agreement on decision rights, board size (five to seven members is typical), and standing committees for finance/audit, compensation, and governance so that “helping the CEO scale” doesn’t quietly become “replacing the CEO.”
